Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.item: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'the people responsible have faced no consequences' is hard to reconcile unless there was a clear perpetrator such as major medical negligence. Nothing else in the profile suggests an interpersonal or negligence-based trauma, so this appraisal appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
issues.explanation: A specific perfume or cologne as a trigger is not impossible, but in the context of life-threatening illness it usually needs some link to a person or setting. Here, the rest of the profile does not support an interpersonal perpetrator or a distinctive sensory cue tied to treatment, making this trigger weakly grounded and less coherent with the other selected items.

vignette:
Claire Martin, a 39-year-old dentist, came to treatment after more than a year of trying to keep a frightening period of illness sealed off from the rest of her life. She spoke about it carefully and sparingly, as if too much detail might pull her back into it. The illness had begun abruptly, with symptoms severe enough that she was admitted to the hospital and told there was a real risk to her life. What stayed with her most was not a single dramatic image but the sense of being trapped inside a body that had become unfamiliar and beyond her control. She remembered lying in a hospital bed surrounded by the sharp antiseptic smell of disinfectant, aware of people moving around her, making decisions, while she felt she had no options of her own. She could not simply get up and leave, could not make her body do what she wanted, and could not reassure herself that she would recover. In those days she had felt cornered by her own physical vulnerability.

After she was discharged, Claire returned to her dental practice, but the experience did not settle into the past in the way she had hoped. The smell of antiseptic, unavoidable in her work, began to catch her off guard. In the operatory, as she cleaned a room between patients or opened fresh supplies, the hospital smell seemed suddenly too close to the one she remembered from her admission. For a moment she would feel herself tighten internally, with the same dread that had accompanied lying in bed and waiting for other people to tell her what would happen next. She did not describe these moments dramatically; what frightened her was how quickly they arrived and how little choice she felt she had in them. The sense of entrapment could also surface in ordinary situations if she perceived herself as having no way out—being hemmed in by a packed schedule at the clinic, stuck in a small room, or feeling unable to step away once a procedure had begun. In those moments she was not just stressed; she was back in contact with that earlier conviction that she had been trapped and defenseless.

Old photographs became difficult in a different way. Pictures from before the illness, or even photos taken around that period, stirred up memories she did not want near her. Sometimes seeing an older image of herself on her phone or in a family album brought an immediate, sickened recognition of the person she had been before her body had failed her so completely. Rather than nostalgia, she felt a jolt of loss. She had come to believe that the illness had changed her permanently for the worse, and photographs seemed to confront her with evidence of someone stronger and less damaged than the person she now took herself to be.

Over the months, Claire narrowed her life in ways that made sense to her at the time. She stopped looking closely at her own body. She avoided mirrors when possible, rushed through dressing, and tried not to notice ordinary physical sensations. Paying attention to her body felt dangerous, as though any close observation might reveal something else going wrong or confirm that she could no longer trust it. She was certain that her body had become unreliable, capable of betraying her without warning, and this made even neutral bodily awareness feel like a risk. She also withdrew from other people. Outside of work, she declined invitations, kept visits brief, and became harder to reach. When her partner tried to ask about the illness or how she had been since, Claire changed the subject or said she was tired. Talking about what happened, or about its aftermath, felt exposing and intolerable. She did not want to hear herself describe how frightened she had been, and she did not want other people looking at her as someone fragile.

These changes began to affect her relationships and her work. At the practice, Claire remained competent and meticulous, but she structured her day to minimize unnecessary contact, keeping conversations with colleagues focused and brief. At home, her partner experienced her as increasingly distant. Claire knew this, but she also felt ashamed. She had come to believe the illness revealed something fundamental about her—that she was a weak person. The fact that reminders still unsettled her seemed, to her, to prove it. She judged herself harshly for not having simply moved on.

By the time she sought help, what finally pushed her to come in was a recent moment at work when the smell of antiseptic in a treatment room and the feeling of being unable to step away from a patient combined so strongly that she felt inwardly frozen for several minutes afterward. She completed the appointment, but the experience left her shaken. She said she was tired of organizing her life around not seeing, not smelling, not talking, and not noticing. At the same time, she was afraid that therapy might confirm what she already believed—that she had been permanently damaged by the illness and could no longer rely on herself. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was to be able to be in her own body again without fear and to move through her work and her relationship without feeling that the hospital was always just beneath the surface.
